required_evidence: no evidence transfer from Turso Database profiles

operations.notes: The v1 graph orchestrator is qualified only on SQLite; other backends do not register an implementation.
Ownership recovery is currently implemented only by the SQLite/default MCP runtime.

The advisory preflight is implemented through backend-owned read snapshots and exercised by the shared portable facet scenario on supported physical adapters, but remains intentionally unqualified until backend full-proof declarations and receipts land.

Postgres and Turso-local share the bounded live structured pipeline. Historical projection, activity terminals, interpretation and federated-Message provenance enrichment, and governed comments fail closed.
Exact-name batch resolution is qualified only on SQLite; other backends withhold the operation.
Postgres and Turso-local evaluate stored live rollups in the admitted read snapshot and report cache_hit=false; revision receipts, revision-keyed caching, and fencing are not claimed.

Postgres and Turso-local execute backend-native lexical candidate selection in the admitted snapshot, then share caller/no-oracle filtering, scopes, ranking/ties, shaping, caps, freshness, and replay semantics. They remain Partial because English/Porter/Turso tokenization and stemming are not implementation-identical, snippets are shared deterministic match windows rather than engine-native fragments, and prefix/infix/sibling near misses use the bounded authorized catalogue rather than a proved physical prefix index.

Postgres uses a pinned exhaustive AST validator, a per-call discarded least-privilege role session, and caller-filtered security-barrier projections. Turso local executes exact-parser-qualified SELECTs only against a bounded caller-visible MemoryIO projection, with core query-only, progress, deadline, and interrupt controls.
Postgres and Turso-local implement census, provenance, authorship, recent, relationship, container, and convergence axes; lexical scan fails closed and remains a search qualification.
SQLite owns the append-authoritative durable activity lifecycle. Other request adapters do not advertise closure parity.
Physical SQLite snapshots do not cross profiles; Turso local is conversion-intended but has no current proof or qualified file fast path.
Hosted membership administration belongs to the host catalog plane, not the selected content backend.
The federated gateway owns this tool; destination writes still require a separately qualified backend route.
The interaction tap is optional and must be explicitly suppressed when unsupported.
Account-scoped custody is currently an owner-controlled local filesystem store outside workspace databases.
The reconciler joins the SQLite catalog membership plane to workspace-local bindings and account-scoped custody.
Fleet migration planning currently enumerates managed SQLite database files only.
Fleet migration execution currently operates on managed SQLite database files only.
Fleet migration status currently scans managed SQLite database files only.
The reset path currently removes explicitly named managed SQLite tenant files under hosting-catalog safeguards.
The disposable-tenant reset currently targets one managed SQLite tenant file.
The disposable-fleet reset currently targets three managed SQLite tenant files.
Challenge purge is a hosting-catalog operation rather than a selected content-backend operation.
Empty-state verification is owned by the SQLite hosting catalog and managed database directory.
The exact-release staging bootstrap initializes only an empty local SQLite catalog and authorizes no deployment, migration, reset, or production operation.
Fencing an account for deletion is a hosting-catalog transaction over accounts, memberships and credentials rather than a selected content-backend operation.
The purge destroys managed SQLite database files on the local volume and their backup generations before tombstoning the catalog identity.
Cancelling a fenced deletion restores a managed SQLite database file from the configured backup sink.
Fencing an owner-created workspace is a hosting-catalog authority transition; the selected content backend is not touched until purge.
Workspace purge destroys managed SQLite database files, backup generations and local routing handles after the recovery window.
Cancelling workspace retirement returns a managed SQLite database to service and repairs a missing file only from the configured backup sink.
